title: The Girl Who Can
author: Ama Ata Aidoo
tagline: Seven-year-old Adjoa's thin legs, her grandmother's worries, and a running trophy that changes what the family sees.

overview.intro: Adjoa, seven years old, grows up in a Ghanaian household where her grandmother Nana measures her legs — literally and figuratively — against ideas about what a woman should be. Adjoa does not fully understand the adults' discussions about her body, but she understands results: at school she runs faster than anyone, wins a trophy for her school, and brings it home. Aidoo tells the story in a child's clear, puzzled, funny voice, so that a large subject — how society judges girls' bodies and futures — arrives disguised as everyday family life.

learn.title: Before you read: a child's-eye story

blocks.text: Ama Ata Aidoo writes from within Ghanaian women's experience, and this story is one of her clearest studies of how expectations are passed down through generations. In Adjoa's household, remarks about the girl's thin legs are never explained to her, yet she records them with a child's precision. The gap between what the adults mean and what Adjoa understands is where the story's comedy and its criticism both live.

As you read, keep two lists: what the adults say Adjoa's legs are for, and what Adjoa actually does with them. The plot's pleasure comes from the moment the two lists collide, and the ending's humour comes from watching Nana rearrange her opinions without ever admitting that she was wrong.

Seven-year-old Adjoa narrates life with her mother, Maami, and her grandmother, Nana. She gradually realises that Nana considers her legs too thin and worries aloud that they will not suit her for adult womanhood and motherhood. Adjoa cannot follow all the adult conversation, but she understands that her body is being discussed and found wanting. At school, a different measurement applies: she can run, and she can run well enough to be chosen to represent her school at a district sports meeting.

items: Nana's comments about thin legs form a running background hum through Adjoa's home life.
At school the legs are assessed by what they can do, not by how they look.
Adjoa is selected for the district sports event — the first time her ability matters publicly.
She runs well and wins a trophy for her school.
Nana receives the trophy with pride and carries it home, her earlier worries quietly overturned.
The ending echoes Nana's own words back at her: the legs that were 'too thin' have done something notable.

items.text: Nana discusses Adjoa's legs in adult terms that Adjoa half-hears and records literally.
items.note: The child narrator reports the worry accurately but cannot report its meaning — the reader supplies the critique.

items.text: The trophy goes home in Nana's keeping.
items.note: The object of family pride is won by the very body the family doubted: the story's argument in one image.

blocks.text: Adjoa is observant, literal and entirely without self-pity. She does not complain about the comments on her legs; she notes them the way a child notes weather. Her narration is reliable about events and unreliable about meanings, which is Aidoo's central device: we understand the injustice before Adjoa does. Her ambition is simple and public — she wants to run — and her achievement is proportionate to her age, a school trophy rather than a grand victory, which keeps the story honest.

Nana is the household's guardian of tradition: she measures girls against ideas she inherited, about womanhood, marriage and motherhood. She is not cruel — her worry is genuine — but it is a worry that narrows a child's future before the child has lived into it. Her change of heart is funny because it is unacknowledged: she does not concede an error, she simply becomes proud, and pride lets her claim the trophy as a family inheritance. Maami, Adjoa's mother, belongs to the conversation between them, the middle generation that passes the talk along without necessarily agreeing with it.

items.meaning: Seven-year-old narrator; observant, literal, and a natural runner.
Grandmother; guardian of traditional expectations who judges Adjoa's legs and later claims her trophy.
Adjoa's mother, part of the adult discussions about the child's body and future.
The running prize that changes how the household measures Adjoa's legs.
A story told by a child who reports accurately but understands only part of the adult meaning.

blocks.text: The story's main subject is gender expectation: Nana evaluates Adjoa's body by what it is presumed to be for, years before Adjoa could possibly know. Aidoo shows how such judgments are delivered casually, in talk over a child's head, and how completely they can limit a girl's imagined future. The counterweight is ability: at school Adjoa's legs are assessed by performance, and performance gives a verdict the family's talk cannot overrule.

The story also weighs generations. Nana's standards come from her own lifetime; Adjoa's possibilities come from hers; and the trophy sits between them as proof that the standards can be outgrown. Because the narrator is a child, none of this is argued — it is shown. The reader does the arguing, which is exactly Aidoo's intention: the critique of limiting expectations arrives gently, through laughter, rather than as a lecture.

items: Gender expectations: a girl's body judged by presumed future roles rather than present ability.
Ability and agency: running lets Adjoa define herself instead of being defined.
Generational change: Nana's pride shows tradition adapting when confronted with evidence.
Education and opportunity: school is where Adjoa's legs are given a fair measurement.
Child versus adult understanding: the reader sees the injustice before the narrator does.

blocks.text: First-person child narration is the story's engine. Adjoa reports exactly what is said — including comments no seven-year-old should have to interpret — and her literalness makes the adult talk visible in its full absurdity. She also supplies unintentional comedy: her puzzled summaries of grown-up conversation are funny without meaning to be, and her simple account of the race carries the excitement of a child for whom this is the biggest event of her life.

items: The title itself is the story's thesis: 'who can' — ability — set against 'who is' — appearance.
Repetition of the leg remarks gives the story its rhythm and makes the trophy's answer cumulative.
The humour is warm rather than cruel: Nana is corrected by events, not by ridicule.

learn.title: Reading and writing tips for this story

blocks.text: Answers about this story should always mention narration: the child's voice is not decoration, it is how the theme is delivered. For character questions on Nana, show the arc — worry, judgment, then unacknowledged pride — and quote her reactions to both the legs and the trophy. For theme questions, keep the contrast between the two measurements (appearance at home, ability at school) at the centre of your answer.

items: Use the phrase 'dramatic irony' precisely: Adjoa does not understand what the reader understands.
When asked about the ending, explain the humour AND the change in Nana — both are marked.
Avoid judging Nana as a villain; the story treats her as a product of her generation, which is subtler.
Anchor every generalisation about gender expectation in one concrete incident from the household.

keyPoints: The story is narrated by seven-year-old Adjoa, whose literal voice exposes adult prejudice without labelling it.
Nana judges Adjoa's legs by appearance and imagined womanhood; the school judges them by what they can do.
Dramatic irony is the central device: the reader grasps the unfairness before Adjoa does.
The trophy is the story's turning point — proof, made of metal, that the doubted legs can achieve.
Nana never admits she was wrong; her unacknowledged pride is the source of the ending's gentle humour.
Themes: gender expectation, ability and agency, generational change, and the power of education and sport.
Aidoo's tone is warm and comic rather than angry, which lets the critique travel further.
The title states the theme: ability ('who can') challenged against appearance ('who is').
The middle generation (Maami) shows how such expectations are transmitted in ordinary family talk.
examFocus: Narration question: explain how a child's reportage creates irony — give one example of what Adjoa says and what the reader understands.
Nana's character: track worry → judgment → pride, and note that her change is never stated aloud.
Theme answers must contrast the two measurements of Adjoa: appearance at home, performance at school.
Style: discuss warmth and humour; the story critiques through laughter, not invective.
The ending: the trophy's reception carries the whole argument — be ready to write a paragraph on it.
Do not import invented quotations; work from incidents and paraphrase, as the exam expects.

questions.prompt: What worries Nana has about Adjoa?
options: That Adjoa's legs are too thin to suit her for adult womanhood and motherhood
That Adjoa is falling behind in her schoolwork
That Adjoa spends too much time indoors reading
That Adjoa has no interest in learning to cook
questions.answer: That Adjoa's legs are too thin to suit her for adult womanhood and motherhood
questions.explanation: Nana's repeated concern is about Adjoa's legs and what they promise for her future as a woman. The worry is stated in adult terms over a child's head, which is exactly how Adjoa comes to hear of it.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing a school-related worry — Nana's comments are about the body and its presumed future, not studies.

questions.prompt: How do Adjoa's legs get assessed at school?
options: By a medical examination that confirms Nana's worries
By what they can do — she runs well and is chosen to represent the school
By a teacher's comment on their appearance in the school photograph
They are never assessed; the school ignores her completely
questions.answer: By what they can do — she runs well and is chosen to represent the school
questions.explanation: At school the measurement changes from appearance to performance: running ability earns Adjoa selection for the district sports event. This second measurement is the one that finally answers the first.
questions.commonMistake: Forgetting the selection — the race is not an isolated event; being chosen is part of the school's judgement.

questions.prompt: What happens after Adjoa wins the district sports event?
questions.answer: Adjoa wins a trophy for her school, and the trophy comes home with the family. Nana, who had worried most about Adjoa's legs, receives it with pride and carries it herself, openly claiming the achievement as part of the family's honour.
questions.explanation: Two movements are needed: the public win (trophy for the school) and the private reception (Nana's pride, carrying it home). Together they complete the story's reversal.
questions.commonMistake: Stopping at the race itself — the story's point is made in the household's response, not the race.

questions.prompt: How does Nana's attitude towards Adjoa's legs change by the end of the story?
questions.answer: At the start Nana treats the legs as a flaw — too thin to suit the future she imagines for Adjoa. By the end, after the trophy, the same legs are a source of family pride, and Nana carries the prize home as if she had always believed in them. The change is never stated or admitted: it simply happens when the evidence arrives.
questions.explanation: The answer must show the direction of the change (flaw → pride) and its manner (unacknowledged). Nana does not apologise or argue; events move her opinion silently.
questions.commonMistake: Claiming Nana apologises — the text gives her pride, not confession, and the humour depends on that.

questions.prompt: Explain how Aidoo uses Adjoa's child narration to criticise the adults' attitudes. Illustrate from the story.
questions.answer: Adjoa reports what she hears without grasping its full meaning, so the reader hears the adult talk in its raw form and supplies the criticism herself. When Nana worries aloud about thin legs and womanhood, Adjoa simply records the words — but the reader recognises a child's body being judged by adult standards she has not even reached. Her literalness also deflates the talk: unable to follow the discussion, she makes it visible as puzzling obsession rather than wisdom. Because the narrator never accuses anyone, the critique cannot be dismissed as a quarrel; it emerges from the gap between what Adjoa says and what the events prove.
questions.explanation: The device to name is dramatic irony through child narration: accurate reporting, incomplete understanding. Each illustration should show the gap — Adjoa's literal report versus the reader's recognition.
questions.commonMistake: Saying Aidoo 'uses a child to make it simple' — the child's voice complicates the adults' talk; it does not simplify it.

questions.prompt: How does the story contrast life at home with life at school for Adjoa?
questions.answer: At home Adjoa is measured by appearance and by what her body is presumed to be for: Nana's comments judge her legs against an imagined future of womanhood and motherhood, in conversations Adjoa is not meant to follow. At school the measurement is performance — she runs, she is selected, she wins. The two settings therefore offer two definitions of a girl's worth, and the plot lets the second answer the first: the trophy cannot be argued with, and it walks back into the house under Nana's own arm. The contrast is the story's structure as much as its theme.
questions.explanation: Strong answers name the two criteria (appearance versus ability), give one incident from each setting, and show how the plot moves the school's verdict into the home.
questions.commonMistake: Describing home and school without naming the different criteria — the contrast is evaluative, not merely locational.

questions.prompt: Discuss the theme of changing generational attitudes in the story.
questions.answer: The story stages three generations: Nana, whose standards were inherited from her own time; Maami, who transmits the household's talk; and Adjoa, whose possibilities belong to her own era. Change is shown rather than argued: Nana's doubts are outgrown by the child's achievements, and her pride at the trophy reveals a tradition bending without ever admitting it moved. Aidoo presents the shift warmly — no one is denounced — which suggests her view that attitudes change when new evidence (education, sport, opportunity) walks through the door carrying a prize. Crucially, the change comes from Adjoa's doing, not from argument: the story trusts achievement to rewrite expectation.
questions.explanation: A discussion of generational attitudes needs the three positions (inherited standards, transmitted talk, new possibilities) and a judgement about how change occurs in this story — by evidence, not confrontation.
questions.commonMistake: Focusing only on Nana — the generational theme involves the line of transmission through Maami as well.

questions.prompt: Why is it significant that it is Nana who carries the trophy home?
questions.answer: Nana is the person who doubted Adjoa's legs most, so her carrying the prize turns the story's judgement upside down in a single image. The trophy becomes her public proof of pride, even though she never retracts her earlier words — the object speaks the apology she will not.
questions.explanation: Significance questions ask why a particular detail matters: identify who Nana is (the chief critic) and what the act expresses (unspoken reversal), then connect the two.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the scene without explaining why Nana specifically matters — the choice of carrier is the point.

questions.prompt: Is the story's ending a victory for Adjoa, for Nana, or for both? Discuss with close reference to the plot.
questions.answer: For Adjoa it is a clear victory: her legs, the subject of domestic doubt, are publicly validated, and she returns with the trophy that cannot be reinterpreted. Her achievement is her own — she ran, she won — and the story gives her no self-congratulation, only the child's simple account, which makes the victory dignified. For Nana it is also, arguably, a victory: she carries the trophy home as family honour, absorbing her granddaughter's achievement into her own standards without ever conceding an error. Whether that satisfies depends on what one wants for Adjoa — the family gains pride, but not necessarily understanding. The strongest reading holds both: the ending wins Adjoa her future and gives Nana her comfort, and Aidoo leaves the deeper question — whether Nana's attitude, as opposed to her behaviour, has changed — gently open. That ambiguity is the story's final irony.
questions.explanation: A discuss question wants both candidates examined and a defended judgement. Evidence: Adjoa's earned win versus Nana's unrepentant pride; the open tone of the close supports a qualified, two-sided verdict.
questions.commonMistake: Declaring a single winner without argument — the question is built for a balanced, evidenced position.

questions.prompt: The title is 'The Girl Who Can'. What can Adjoa do, and what does the title challenge? Write a considered response.
questions.answer: Literally, Adjoa can run — fast enough to win a district event and a trophy for her school. The title sets that ability ('who can') against the household's way of judging her ('who is'): Nana evaluates what Adjoa is — a girl with thin legs, a future body, a presumed role — while the story answers with what she does. Each use of 'can' in the story widens: she can run, she can win, she can change what her family sees, and by implication she can become whatever her ability carries her towards. The title therefore challenges every fixed idea imposed on a child before her life has started, and it does so in the confident, plain grammar of a child herself. It also quietly includes Nana: by the end the reader may ask whether Nana 'can' admit she was wrong — and the trophy suggests she would rather be proud than corrected.
questions.explanation: Title questions reward literal and figurative readings plus a judgement about effect. The literal ability (running) anchors the figurative challenge (doing versus being), and the final twist about Nana shows full command of the story.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only 'she can run' — the mark is for what the title says about the world the story describes.
